<reason>A controlled the decisive axis from Rebuttal 1 onward. B's opening conceded floors are legitimate ("minimum standards can be honest and general"), and A converted that into a dilemma B never escaped: every harm B pressed — rigidity, thin-margin firms priced out, imposition on non-consenters — applies equally or worse to the uniform statutory minimum B endorsed. B's counter was an elegant legitimacy distinction (public law vs. exported private bargain, "industrial regulation wearing a bargaining mask"), but A neutralized it directly: statutes bind strangers too, with no negotiation at all, so on B's own consent test the general minimum "fails harder." That left the economic comparison, where A's calibration argument (differentiated, revisable, industry-negotiated floors vs. one blunt number spanning B's own hotel-kitchen/hospital-cafeteria examples) stood unanswered — B's closing repeated the law/bargain line rather than explaining why a uniform national floor bends better. B's client-liability answer to the cleaner question was legitimate but arrived only in Rebuttal 2, underdeveloped, and A plausibly framed it as an admission the bare number was insufficient. Both sides were disciplined (no fake citations, plausible background examples), both asked sharp pressure questions and answered with proper A1/A2 structure, and B was arguably the better stylist. But B's job-loss mechanism proved too much against its own alternative, and its best frame was subsumed by A's "both impose — choose the better imposition" reframe. A made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 1 turn of B's concession [A2.1]: showing that B's entire rigidity/imposition critique indicts the uniform statutory minimum B defended more than tailored sectoral floors — a dilemma A sharpened in A4.4 ("a floor high enough to matter carries that risk; one low enough to be riskless protects nobody") and sealed in the closing by turning B's own hotel-kitchen/hospital-cafeteria examples against the one-size-fits-all alternative. B's strongest counter-thrust (law is supposed to bind strangers; a bargain is not) was clean but never resolved the economic comparison.</best_rebuttal>
